title: CLEAR: Legible and Steerable Recommendation via Grounded Natural-Language Interests
summary: Modern recommenders keep learned preferences in representations people cannot inspect or change. We present CLEAR (Controllable and Legible End-to-end Architecture for Recommendation), an end-to-end system deployed at Meta and built around an editable natural-language interest layer. CLEAR makes a ranked subset of inferred interests readable and stores accepted additions and suppressions as authoritative preference state. Behavioral grounding maps each inferred interest back to supporting events in the user's own history. The resulting interest object is also a serving address: its label and profile-conditioned rewrites drive lexical retrieval, its supporting events seed behavioral retrieval, its projection queries an embedding index, and its stable identity supports ranking, attribution, and exposure control. A fresh user declaration may precede behavioral support, so it enters through the same serving identity and initially draws candidates from topical retrieval. Ranking makes those candidates competitive, while a delivery controller observes attributable exposure and replenishes underexposed interests. Direct user review found that users rated about 88.5% of displayed interests accurate. In an offline benchmark using a shared evaluation protocol, the Specialized 3B generator reached 0.3967 mean-user F1@10, compared with 0.3633 for Gemini 2.5 Pro and 0.1911 for the prior generator. For a newly declared interest, a user-randomized cumulative ablation measured same-day delivery losses of 8.7 percentage points for added-interest ranking terms, 11.1 for reserved top-slot insertion, and 13.7 for interest-conditioned candidate sourcing, conditional on the tested removal sequence. CLEAR components have operated in production for over one year; the system spans four surfaces on Instagram and Facebook, with an interest layer people can inspect, correct, and use to direct recommendations.

title: Confidence Without Cause: Predicting and Localizing Physics-Shortcut Sensitivity in Language Model Hidden States
summary: A language model's confidence on a physics problem deserves trust only if it ignores details irrelevant to the answer. We introduce DECOY (Distractor-Embedded Certified cOunterfactuals for phYsics): 155 families of four prompts differing in one irrelevant detail. A symbolic solver certifies that each edit preserves the answer. Families are labelled by the largest drop in the model's log-probability of the certified answer, using a threshold fixed before probe training. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is sensitive on 50.0% of the 140 families yielding labels, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 22.9%. Effects are largest when distractor values lie numerically close to the answer. A linear probe on Qwen's layer-18 hidden state, averaged over four renderings, predicts sensitivity before generation at AUROC 0.760 with whole families held out. A separately tuned single-rendering probe reaches 0.747. A frozen layer-16 probe reaches 0.820 pooled AUROC on 15 families built after training, though within-cue-type AUROC is lower (0.667-0.6875). Under a paired family bootstrap, the probe performs on par with a fitted token-entropy baseline (AUROC 0.727) and achieves the lowest Brier score among tested predictors (0.204 versus 0.214). Knocking out four attention heads at layer 16 cancels sensitivity on a 20-family panel, localising it to a narrow mechanism. These results show that Qwen's confidence can track irrelevant details, that this failure is detectable before generation, and that targeted intervention can suppress it. DECOY provides certified ground truth and paired-tested baselines for evaluating hidden-state monitors.

title: Size-Matched Nulls Reveal What Block Ablation Measures in MambaVision
summary: Hybrid vision backbones interleave Mamba state-space mixers with self-attention, and a block's role is usually probed by removing it and measuring the damage. We test what that measurement means in MambaVision. On all 50,000 ImageNet validation images and three model sizes, every block ablation is paired with a size-matched null, the same perturbation with its channels shuffled or their signs flipped. In top-1 accuracy and in true-class rank, real and null damage are nearly indistinguishable in absolute terms: pooled over the blocks of MambaVision-T, the content effect lies within [-0.044,+0.016] percentage points (90% interval). Two attention-only controls show that the test detects content, with real ablations worse than their nulls by up to 4.2 points in DeiT-Small and 1.0 point in Swin-T. Part of MambaVision's near-equivalence reflects how little damage its blocks do (0.11--0.34 points on average, against 1.7 and 2.1). Scaled by damage, its content share is comparable to Swin-T's in accuracy, lower in rank, and far below DeiT-Small's: single-block damage in MambaVision is small and mostly positional. Ablation also hides what blocks carry together: removing all blocks of one type compounds damage to 3.7--8.4 times the sum of single effects, far more than size-matched nulls, including nulls that keep the alignment between the blocks' perturbations; for adjacent pairs, aligned nulls reproduce most of it. Freezing input-dependent selection in all Mamba mixers shows that it accounts for 20--32% of the Mamba contribution, mainly through the B and C projections. We turn these results into a protocol for causal attribution in hybrid networks.

title: TokenFormer V2: Breaking the Resolution-Complexity Dilemma in Unified Recommendation
summary: Industrial recommendation faces a resolution--complexity dilemma: dense interactions make detailed modeling of long behavior histories expensive, while compact history summaries restrict the evidence available to prediction. A unified backbone must preserve rich behavioral details within strict serving budgets. We introduce \textbf{TokenFormer V2}, a unified architecture that explicitly decouples \emph{representation resolution} from \emph{interaction density}. Its group-wise token layout jointly encodes behavior segments with non-sequential context, expands interaction ranges via hierarchical group merging, and coordinates distributed groups through \emph{NS Fusion} and \emph{Global Sync} modules. Through this \emph{local--global decomposition} paradigm, computation is concentrated on structured interactions while preserving fine-grained evidence, ensuring that every encoded event remains directly accessible to the \emph{Full-Resolution Readout} module. On the Tencent Advertising Algorithm Competition 2026 (TAAC 2026) benchmark, TokenFormer V2 achieves top-ranking accuracy among unified recommendation baselines while using \textbf{5.1$\times$ fewer FLOPs} than leading baselines, sustaining its advantage across long histories and imbalanced behavior domains. Furthermore, in billion-parameter evaluations on WeChat Channels advertising, it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art industrial baselines, yielding up to a \textbf{+0.07 pp} overall AUC gain. In live online A/B testing against the production model, TokenFormer V2 delivers a statistically significant \textbf{2.33\% increase in GMV}. These results establish TokenFormer V2 as a battle-tested blueprint for scalable, full-resolution behavior modeling in industrial recommendation.

title: Agent-Guided Process Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction
summary: Large language models have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning, yet in complex multi-step reasoning, an error at any step may propagate along an incorrect path, and the resulting solution may omit necessary branches. Existing natural-language reflection methods often struggle to locate critical errors precisely, while outcome verification typically checks only whether the available candidate answers satisfy the problem conditions and can therefore overlook necessary branches. To address these limitations, we propose Agent-Guided Process Verification (AGPV) for mathematical self-correction. AGPV decomposes the current solution into an ordered sequence of key claims, verifies them individually while invoking a shared mathematical toolbox when needed, and stops upon detecting the first error. A summarization agent converts the failure evidence into a diagnosis that guides a correction agent to re-derive the subsequent solution from that point; AGPV then adapts the next verification iteration to the revised solution. AGPV also verifies solution completeness. We further prove that AGPV guarantees solution correctness and completeness when key claims provide sufficient coverage and local verification is reliable, provided that all key claims pass verification. The implementation compresses long working contexts and reuses successful tool results within each problem. We evaluate AGPV on five challenging mathematical reasoning datasets with four models from DeepSeek, Qwen, and GPT. AGPV achieves an average accuracy of 63.8%, outperforming the strongest among the representative baselines evaluated (50.3%) by 13.5 percentage points, with higher repair coverage than the programmatic-verification baselines.

title: Attribution-Guided Shared-Private Decoupling for Noise-Reduced Audio-Visual Representation Learning
summary: Audio-visual representation learning commonly aligns paired audio and visual signals with sample-level contrastive objectives. However, real-world audio-visual pairs usually contain heterogeneous patch tokens: only a subset carries reliable cross-modal shared semantics, while many others mainly encode modality-private residuals. Aggregating all tokens into a single global representation can therefore introduce semantic noise into cross-modal alignment. Motivated by the minimal-sufficiency principle, we propose an attribution-guided shared-private decoupling framework to mitigate this issue. Our key idea is to identify shared-cover subviews that preserve dominant cross-modal information while suppressing modality-private residuals, and use them to supervise decoupled shared and private representations. To identify such subviews efficiently, we draw on transformer attribution method and introduce Layer-Truncated Attribution (LTA), which provides a lightweight estimate of token-level relevance to cross-modal shared information. We further adopt a teacher-student framework, where the teacher provides attribution-induced supervision and the student internalizes shared-private decoupling into its representations, without introducing extra inference cost. Experiments on retrieval, classification, and sound-prompted semantic segmentation show consistent gains over strong baselines. Compared with baseline, our method improves the average zero-shot R@1 by 4.0 across AudioSet and VGGSound retrieval, and improves AS20K classification mAP by 3.1, demonstrating the effectiveness of fine grained attribution guidance for reducing semantic noise.reducing semantic noise. Code will be released at https://github.com/wanglg20/LTA

title: ST-GAT: A Leakage-Free Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Framework for Robust Network Intrusion Detection
summary: Intrusion detection systems are a central defence in modern networks. Deep learning models report strong anomaly-detection results, but evaluations on standard benchmarks such as CSE-CIC-IDS-2018 are often inflated by two methodological problems: temporal leakage from overlapping sliding windows, and contamination from preprocessing fitted before the train/test split. Per-flow classifiers also ignore the spatio-temporal dependencies across sequences of network flows. We propose a Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Network (ST-GAT) that represents traffic as a sequence of graph snapshots. It builds k-Nearest Neighbour (k-NN) edges within each window, applies multi-head Graph Attention Network (GAT) layers for spatial aggregation, and uses a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network with temporal attention for sequence modelling. To prevent leakage, we use non-overlapping temporal windows (stride equal to window length) and fit all preprocessing on the training split only. We compare three class-imbalance strategies: inverse class-frequency weighting, dynamic balanced sampling, and few-shot metric prototyping. Across three random seeds, ST-GAT with inverse class weighting reached a Macro-F1 of 96.65% (+/- 0.87) and an accuracy of 99.14%. This is 14.3 percentage points higher in Macro-F1 than a per-flow Random Forest baseline (82.34%). Balanced sampling reduced Macro-F1 by 2.3 points (to 94.37%) relative to loss weighting. This suggests that aggressive resampling of small, noisy minority classes can hurt detection in heavily imbalanced traffic.

title: A Geometric Understanding of Denoising Autoencoder with Applications to Image Denoising
summary: Denoising autoencoders have shown strong empirical performance in recovering clean data from their noisy observations, yet their underlying statistical behavior remains underexplored. In this paper, we study denoising autoencoders under the manifold hypothesis, assuming that clean data are supported on low-dimensional smooth manifolds embedded in a high-dimensional ambient space, while noisy observations are generated by isotropic Gaussian noise. We establish generalization guarantees in three geometric scenarios: a single manifold, a pairwise separated finite union of manifolds, and a finite union of intersecting manifolds. Using local chart representations, partitions of unity, and neural network approximation, we derive upper bounds for the expected squared reconstruction error for denoising autoencoder. In the single-manifold and separated-union scenarios, the error consists of a sample-dependent statistical term of order $n^{-2/(d+2)}\log^4 n$, a residual term of order $dσ^2/D$ caused by tangential noise, and an exponentially small tail term associated with failure of the manifold projection. Here $D$ is the data ambient dimension, $d$ is the intrinsic dimension of the clean-data manifold, and $σ^2$ is the expected squared noise magnitude. In the scenario of intersecting manifolds, we further identify an additional ambiguity term determined by the probability mass near the intersection neighborhood. Numerical experiments on synthetic manifolds and real image datasets support the predicted sample-size scaling law and illustrate the additional reconstruction ambiguity near manifold intersections.

title: Improving Early Detection of Scientifically Interesting Radio Sources Using Enhanced Isolation Forest
summary: The rapid growth of radio astronomical surveys has created a major challenge in identifying scientifically interesting sources from large populations of observed objects. This study investigates whether enhanced Isolation Forest (iForest) methods can improve the early detection and ranking of scientifically interesting radio sources. Four iForest variants, Standard Enhanced, Pooled Gain, Kurtosis-based, and Hypervolume, are evaluated using 1,031 extended radio sources from the MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy Survey (MGCLS). Each source is represented by a 52-dimensional feature set derived using Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL) self-supervised learning and principal component analysis (PCA), while expert scientific-interest ratings are used to define the ground-truth labels. The methods are evaluated using Average Precision (AP), receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC), Precision@10, Precision@50, and cumulative anomaly detection. Pooled Gain achieves the highest Average Precision (AP = 0.201) and the strongest early-stage ranking performance (P@10 = 0.600), identifying six expert-validated anomalies among the ten highest-ranked sources. Standard Enhanced and Kurtosis-based achieve the highest ROC AUC (0.677), while the AUC values of the four variants range from 0.653 to 0.677. These results indicate that feature-aware isolation strategies can improve the prioritization of scientifically interesting sources at the top of the ranked list, although overall discrimination remains comparable across the evaluated variants. The findings support the use of enhanced Isolation Forest methods as an initial ranking mechanism within human-in-the-loop systems for large-scale radio astronomical surveys.

title: Sharp First-Hit Identification from Finite Depth Samples
summary: Which depths in a new camera view are determined by finitely many source-depth measurements? Pointwise uncertainty bounds do not answer this question: unobserved geometry between samples can change which surface is encountered first. We study a bounded Lipschitz class of continuous source inverse-depth fields with interval observations and known camera pose. Building on classical Lipschitz envelopes, we characterize the exact set of attainable first-hit depths and construct a globally admissible scene for every value in that set. The set can be disconnected. We also give a necessary and sufficient test for several proposed depths to be first hits of one shared scene. An epipolar reduction uses scalar cone inequalities without enumerating surfaces. In a rectified model with source spacing $h$, interval half-width $\varepsilon$, baseline $b$, and slope bound $L$, we prove a sharp worst-case inverse-depth diameter of $\max\{Lh+2\varepsilon,2\varepsilon/(1-bL)\}$ when $bL<1$, subject to sufficient depth and domain range for attainment. Exact samples still give the sharp bound $Lh$ at $bL=1$, while above this threshold ambiguity need not vanish as sampling becomes arbitrarily dense. Any positive measurement uncertainty can destroy uniform stability at the critical threshold. We provide constructive examples, an exact rational validation oracle, and a frozen ten-scene evaluation using reference, stereo, and learned-depth observations. The experiments separate solver correctness under the scene assumptions from failure of those assumptions: fixed learned-depth bands often yield narrow but incorrect sets. The results identify what a specified scene class permits; they do not infer a continuum regularity or physical-scene guarantee from sampled predictions.

title: FundingClaw: Automated Grant Proposal Writing Agents System
summary: Grant proposal writing remains a manual, labor-intensive bottleneck: proposals must satisfy rigid, agency-specific templates, and the same intellectual content must be repeatedly re-encoded into incompatible formats across funding organizations. We introduce FundingClaw, a multi-agent framework built on template-driven skill selection, where a Template Parser ingests any agency's specification and selects the appropriate writing skills for each stage, so that one research brief can produce compliant proposals for NSFC, NSF, KAKENHI, or ERC without modifying generation logic. A blueprint-skeleton strategy drafts a structured outline before any prose is written, mitigating the semantic drift that plagues long-form generation. Three sequential stages produce the rationale, research content, and research foundation sections, with multi-source verification of the PI's record and optional PDF-grounded extraction of representative works. Optional human feedback checkpoints and a closed-loop self-review complete the pipeline. Evaluated on ten research topics with an eight-dimension rubric, FundingClaw outperforms the baseline, narrowing the gap with human level for laborious funding proposal. The code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Objectify, Don't Delete: Complaint-Derived Evaluation of Ambient Clinical Notes
summary: Evaluating the quality of AI-generated clinical notes is hard: standard metrics like ROUGE measure lexical similarity to reference notes, while expert checklists encode what committees believe matters. Neither captures what clinicians actually complain about. Recent work has shown that evaluation criteria can be mined from user feedback and filtered to criteria that LLM judges can reliably enforce. We argue that this is where much of the value is lost. The criteria that fail enforceability are disproportionately the ones clinicians raise most often, because high-frequency complaints are stated as several questions glued together. No yes/no judgment can grade such composites as posed. We introduce an objectification step that rewrites such criteria into sets of scoped, determinate decisions. We demonstrate the approach through an evaluation pipeline that mines criteria from complaints, objectifies them, and deploys LLM judges against both planted defects and production notes. Across eleven defects planted into ACI-bench reference notes, objectified judges localize violations with median recall of 0.95, while reference metrics change by at most 0.037. Given the complaint as one broad question, the same judges still find every planted defect, but they also flag 70% of the unperturbed reference notes; one section-pair question per call raises Youden's J from 0.30 to 0.72 (by 0.19 to 0.26 with prompt effort matched). We release ACI-Defect, a perturbation benchmark; clinician-reviewed instance-level labels showing quality gaps in the ACI-bench gold standard (32 of 40 notes contain hallucinations; 40 of 40 omit discussed facts); and grounding-judge verdicts. On 1,446 production notes, mean instance-rate burden falls at every clinician-rating step (rho=-0.15), a small association. Defect counts have to be kept per span rather than collapsed into one pass/fail bit per note.

title: OmitEHR: Scalable Omission Detection in LLM-Generated Clinical Summaries
summary: Health systems increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to draft summaries of patient medical records, yet evaluations now find omissions, the absence of clinically important information, to be the most common failure mode. Detecting omissions in an LLM-generated summary requires knowing which facts in the record are salient, a signal that existing methods hand-specify, ignore, or recompute at inference with costly LLM judges. We present OmitEHR, a reference-free omission detector that learns clinical salience from historical clinician-written summaries predating widespread LLM use. OmitEHR learns to predict which source-note sentences clinicians include in their summaries, then surfaces high-salience sentences not covered by an LLM-generated summary as candidate omissions. We apply OmitEHR to brief hospital course (BHC) summarization using 5,000 admissions from a large academic medical center. On held-out admissions, OmitEHR outperformed all evaluated baselines at predicting salient source sentences, including a prompted LLM judge. The full omission detection pipeline took 17.7 to 19.5 seconds and cost \$0.03 to \$0.13 per summary depending on the base model, 1.6 to 1.7 times faster and 5.6 to 6.7 times cheaper than scoring every source sentence with an LLM judge. In a blinded review of 25 admissions, two board-certified clinicians confirmed a mean of 5.6 clinically meaningful omissions per summary surfaced by OmitEHR, compared with 3.3 for a full LLM pipeline, counting candidates confirmed by at least one clinician. The efficiency and validity of OmitEHR make it a practical tool for health systems to flag omissions before a summary reaches the clinician.

title: Learning the Average Dose-Response Function with a Right-Censored Treatment
summary: This paper considers estimation and inference for the average dose-response function under right-censored treatment duration and missing outcomes for censored units. Using the duration lower bounds provided by censored records, we construct a novel multiply robust estimator through augmented local estimating equations. Under suitable regularity conditions, the estimator remains consistent when any two of the outcome regression, treatment density, and censoring survival function are consistently estimated. We establish its convergence rate and asymptotic distribution within a cross-fitting framework under appropriate conditions on nuisance estimation. To address local smoothing bias that can distort confidence interval coverage, we further develop a debiased estimator that supports asymptotically valid pointwise inference without undersmoothing. Under additional uniform conditions, we construct simultaneous confidence bands using a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap. Simulation studies evaluate estimation accuracy, the validity of pointwise and uniform inference, and robustness to nuisance model misspecification. A semi-synthetic study calibrated to NHANES illustrates the proposed methods in a setting with a known dose-response function.

title: Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning for Nonstationary Robot Dynamics
summary: Reasoning about what an action will cause requires internalizing how a system behaves. As conditions seldom stay fixed, this must often happen within a few interactions. Yet systems that look identical in a snapshot can respond differently to the same action, depending on physical conditions the snapshot hides. Context-based models capture this separation by summarizing recent transitions into a latent context, but do not specify how that context should change the equations of motion. Physics-informed neural networks build those equations into the model, but describe only a single system and cannot recognize when it has changed. We present Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning (PICR), which bridges the two. Only a context, re-inferred from recent interactions, is updated; it conditions a fixed physics-informed network that determines the robot's inertia and potential energy, so the robot adapts to new physical conditions from its own experience without retraining or a hand-specified robot model. On a Franka Panda arm in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, PICR predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing error on the latter by 1.6-3.8x over baselines, and extends to counterfactual queries under alternative torques. Our analysis shows that the context, inferred solely from interaction, encodes payload physical properties, tracks their changes, and governs the arm's response. The gravity and inertia terms induced by the context further demonstrate its physical validity, each agreeing with the simulator at the level of individual Lagrangian components.

title: dit.xpu : Taming DiT Sparse Inference on Mobile SoCs
summary: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) enable on-device image generation and editing but incur high attention costs at high resolutions. Existing sparse attention reduces computation, yet dynamic sparsity introduces preprocessing and irregular data accesses that poorly fit mobile NPUs. We present DiT.XPU, a sparse DiT inference framework for heterogeneous mobile SoCs. DiT.XPU combines tile-aligned sparse attention with anchor-based error compensation by exploiting slowly varying dense-sparse output residuals across denoising steps. Heterogeneous XPU collaboration overlaps NPU dense attention with GPU sparse calibration, while mask-guided dataflow reduces data transfers and layout conversion by overlapping data movement with computation. Across five DiT models on two Snapdragon smartphones, DiT.XPU achieves up to 1.56x end-to-end denoising speedup over the Hexagon-NPU backend and 11.5x attention-kernel speedup over the fastest alternative, while preserving generation quality close to dense attention. Code is available at https://github.com/IF-LAB-PKU/dit.xpu.

title: Reliable Conditioned Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability via Subsolution Learning on Exact Local Windows
summary: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability computes the maximal safe set and a safety filter for a given obstacle configuration, but it must be re-solved whenever the obstacles change, which a deployed robot cannot afford. Learning a single value function conditioned on the obstacle set removes the re-solve, yet it sharpens the central weakness of learned reachability: one network must now cover a whole family of safety problems, and its approximation error carries no preferred sign, so rare obstacle configurations silently produce false-safe states. To address these challenges, we present a conditioned reachability model designed so that the remaining error falls on the conservative side. Specifically, our method caps the obstacle margin, which makes the value function provably local, in the sense that obstacles farther than a known threshold cannot affect it, so the model reads only a body-frame window, trains on small scenes, and transfers to scenes of any size with millisecond per-scene preparation. Moreover, the output structure builds the value bound into the model. By training with counterexample mining over the finite-dimensional window configuration space, we maximize the claimed safe volume subject to the HJ inequality, so the learned set grows toward the true safe set from the conservative side. Across all tested obstacle settings, ours is the only method that combines recovery comparable to per-scene DeepReach training with near-zero rollout collisions. We also extend the method to a 10D quadrotor, again with markedly lower collision rates than the baselines.

title: Inquest: Log-Guided Root-Cause Code Localization with a Staged Agent
summary: When a production issue is reported, engineers get a description and some logs, but no failing test and no way to reproduce the fault. The logs show where the failure was noticed, not where it was caused: in 49% of the real reports we study, the text names none of the files that the fix later changed. We built a benchmark for this setting from two public datasets and 27 open-source projects (Apache, Red Hat, MongoDB, MariaDB, Qt and Sakai). It holds 38,001 resolved issue reports with their pasted logs, the code as it was while the bug was still present, and the files the fix changed. We present INQUEST, an agent that finds the faulty code using a 27B open-weights model. Code, not the model, controls the procedure. It first gathers the evidence, including the files fixed in similar past issues that were resolved before the report was filed. The model then makes only three bounded decisions: which files to open, what role each file plays in the failure, and how to rank them. On 26,544 evaluation reports, INQUEST ranks a changed file first for 68.6% and in the top five for 85.9%, names the correct module for 90.2%, and ranks a changed function first for 53.8%. On the reports that name no faulty file, it reaches 52.8% and 73.6%. A free agent loop with the same model and tools finds files equally well, but names the faulty function 14 points less often. On a 1,000-report sample, INQUEST beats our reimplementations of two published agents by 7 and 20 points of top-1 accuracy (4 and 16 counting only the reports those agents answered), and the same model used as a re-ranker by 6. We report the cost of every system and the results that go against us, and we release the benchmark, both systems and every run transcript.

title: Robust Well-Log Reconstruction Across Point Gaps and Whole Wells via Boundary-Gated Soft-Thresholding Kalman Fusion
summary: Missing wireline logs hinder subsurface characterization. Deep reconstruction networks suffer from gap-boundary steps and cross-basin shifts, while interpolation and Gaussian smoothers struggle with long intervals and outliers. We propose boundary-gated soft-thresholding Kalman fusion (ST-KF), unifying multiresolution wavelet shrinkage, distance-gated residual prior learning, and closed-form robust Kalman smoothing with learning--inference decoupling. Across two public benchmarks totaling 263 wells in the Norwegian North Sea and New Zealand's Taranaki Basin, ST-KF ranks first over 0.15--100-m anchored gaps with 0.09% parameter overhead. Against the strongest of nine baselines, pooled RMSE falls by 5.0%--8.3% for bulk density and 6.4%--15.6% for compressional slowness; against the four strongest baselines, reductions are 0.7%--4.1% for neutron porosity and 1.3%--2.9% for photoelectric factor. Ablations and sensitivity analyses confirm operator synergy and stable performance: removing state-space fusion increases short-gap errors by up to 58.8%, while zero-shot transfer cuts anchored errors by 14%--68%. The results show that local borehole continuity transfers across basins whereas cross-property mappings shift with regional geology, supporting measurement-guided log reconstruction.

title: Multi-Objective Causal Bandits: Minimal Intervention Space and Policy-Level Learning
summary: Many decision-making problems involve multiple objectives, where actions affect several performance metrics, fairness criteria, or safety constraints. We study multi-objective causal bandits with multiple reward nodes, where actions correspond to interventions on subsets of variables in a causal graph and performance is evaluated through Pareto optimality. Existing approaches to multi-objective bandits often rely on pairwise Pareto dominance or optimize a fixed scalarization. However, pairwise comparisons alone can fail to identify actions dominated by randomized policies, whose expected reward vectors lie in the convex hull of action-level rewards. Thus, an intervention may be suboptimal even if no single intervention dominates it, because it can be dominated by a randomized policy over other interventions. We formalize this policy-level phenomenon and show that it has consequences for both causal action-space reduction and online learning. First, we provide a necessary-and-sufficient graphical characterization of possibly Pareto- optimal minimal intervention sets. Our characterization yields a minimal, sound, and complete candidate intervention family from the graph alone, correcting prior formulations that may include intervention sets that are never Pareto-optimal under any compatible structural causal model. Second, over this reduced intervention space, we design an online UCB-style algorithm that eliminates actions using dominance tests against convex combinations of other actions, and prove logarithmic gap-dependent Pareto regret. Finally, we study constrained multi-objective causal bandits, where feasibility and optimality may be realized only with randomized policies, and develop an online UCB-style constrained bandit algorithm with sublinear regret and constraint-violation guarantees.

title: The Critic Can Hurt: On the Safety of Critics in LLM-Guided AutoML Search
summary: LLM critics increasingly steer iterative search in agentic AutoML, prompt optimization, and self-refinement--evaluated for whether they help, but rarely for whether they can hurt. We isolate the critic's marginal effect through a four-arm audit and characterize the loop's tolerance through controlled fault injection. We show a naive 8B critic drives search below the no-critic random-search floor on 7 of 8 tabular datasets, losing up to 0.245 AUC in the worst case; the magnitude varies strongly with dataset, frontier, and budget. When: stronger critics attenuate the loss on the evaluated suite, without establishing a universal capability threshold. Why: controlled fault injection shows that non-directional errors are nearly costless under best-so-far search, whereas directional errors consume finite search opportunities; an idealized effective-sample calculation yields a necessary condition, $q(m-1) > β$, not a deployment certificate. How: a simple observable validation gate and a learned detector can reduce realized loss, but neither is guaranteed to preserve the full-budget no-critic baseline. We will release CRITFAULT, to our knowledge the first benchmark for detecting harmful critic feedback in AutoML. A critic is not a free addition: audit before trusting, and gate when capability or verification is insufficient.

title: Hard or Mislabeled? Failure Screens Enrich Vision Benchmarks for Label Errors
summary: Hard vision benchmarks often keep images that strong classifiers get wrong. Since a classifier is also marked wrong when the label is wrong, such failure screens may collect label errors. We measure this on ImageNet's twice-relabeled validation set with 103 classifiers. Among the 1,892 images that all 66 supervised classifiers get wrong, 61% have a wrong label, versus 11.1% overall. The fewer images a screen lets through, the more of them are mislabeled, along approximately one curve. Fit on one model family, this curve predicts the screens of two held-out model families with a mean error of 2.4 percentage points, and replays of ImageNet-D's and ImageNet-Hard's screens within 0.1 and 6.3 points. On new pools, ImageNet-V2 and CIFAR-10, enrichment at the strictest screens is stronger than the curve predicts: on ImageNet-V2, by human relabeling, 67% of the images that all 66 classifiers get wrong are mislabeled, against 46% predicted. Screens that let models choose among only some of the classes, as ImageNet-A's does (200 of 1,000), fall below the curve. By ReImageNet, 32% of ImageNet-Hard's ImageNet images have no correct label. ScreenAudit, which comprises an audit tool, a script that rebuilds corrected answer sets for the 5,464 decided ImageNet-Hard images (of 5,646) from ReImageNet's gated release, and per-image audits of 1,198 benchmark images, will be released later.

title: Beyond Paired Inputs: Learning to Leverage RGB-T Cross-Modal Relations in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: RGB and thermal infrared (TIR) sensors provide complementary observations, yet their distinct sensing characteristics make effective cross-modal coordination challenging. Although existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can process paired RGB-T inputs, they often fail to translate cross-modal relations into effective task-specific decisions, leaving the potential of these relations to improve task performance and robustness largely untapped. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RelMLLM, an RGB-T MLLM that explicitly learns to exploit cross-modal relations in task-specific decision making. It represents modality reliability, the cross-modal relation, and the dominant modality as a verifiable decision state. We derive task-grounded supervision for this state by comparing RGB-only, TIR-only, and paired RGB-T task outcomes. A hierarchical relation-guided reward supervises modality-specific evidence, relation-state prediction, and the final task output, while encouraging consistency across evidence, relation, and decision. We evaluate RelMLLM on natural RGB-T grounding, RGB-T visual question answering, and held-out sensor degradation. RelMLLM improves grounding accuracy and degradation robustness over its Qwen3-VL baselines while preserving performance on general RGB-T reasoning benchmarks. These results demonstrate that effectively exploiting cross-modal relations leads to more accurate and robust RGB-T decisions. Code and model weights are publicly available.

title: DynaDFlash: Dynamic Feature Projection for Block Diffusion Speculators
summary: DFlash trains a parallel draft model on hidden features from its target model. Inspired by the previous work of DFlare that introduced per layer combinations of target hidden states, we test whether context dependent weighting of these states helps improve acceptance length of block diffusion speculators. We trained both a DFlash baseline for the Qwen 3 of block size 16, and a dynamic model that computes gates for each layer to affect the magnitude of hidden features before projection. While mean acceptance length between the dynamic model and the DFlash baseline didn't significantly differ, we notice that the dynamic model excels for drafting in the context of math. In an evaluation of 700 prompts from the MetaMathQA and Orca-Math datasets, the mean accepted length improves by 5%. We also found this lead to a 4.1% higher throughput for a subset of the same dataset in the context of speculative decoding.

title: DBHiCo: Dual-Branch Hierarchical Contrastive Learning for MRI Image Classification
summary: Automated Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) image classification provides a crucial non-invasive approach for neurological diagnosis, yet it is fundamentally challenged by inherent acquisition noise and high inter-subject structural similarity, which obscure subtle pathological variations, thereby limiting the performance of deep neural networks. While contrastive learning (CL) offers a promising mitigation strategy, existing paradigms rely on rigid binary partitions that ignore negative sample heterogeneity, and they fail to capture the cross-view structural consistency vital for fine-grained anatomical alignment. To address these barriers, we propose Dual-Branch Hierarchical Contrastive Learning (DBHiCo), a novel framework explicitly designed to collaboratively enforce structural consistency and semantic discrimination. Specifically, DBHiCo leverages a natural anatomical multi-view pair (original and skull-stripped MRI scans), processing them through a dual-branch architecture to seamlessly integrate holistic structural robustness with localized intracranial details. Crucially, we introduce a hierarchical contrastive loss that discards conventional binary constraints in favor of a margin-ranked similarity hierarchy. This mechanism explicitly orders positive and negative pairs based on their structural and semantic difficulty, thereby amplifying the fine-grained semantic discriminability of the learned representations. Extensive experiments across three diverse neurological datasets demonstrate that DBHiCo achieves state-of-the-art performance, consistently outperforming existing MRI multi-view representation learning and advanced contrastive fine-tuning methods.

title: MarineSparkLM-4B: A Lightweight Language Model for Marine and Offshore Engineering Built by Parameter-Efficient Adaptation
summary: Marine and offshore engineering text is spread across preprints, open-access journals, encyclopedias and institutional documents, and the amount of it is small by pretraining standards. We ask how far a lightweight language model for marine and offshore engineering can be taken with parameter-efficient adaptation on a single workstation-class device. Starting from the 4-billion-parameter OceanGPT-basic-4B-Instruct, we train two independent LoRA adapters, each updating 33.0 million of 4.06 billion parameters (0.81%). Training took 4 hours 40 minutes for the first adapter and 10 minutes for the second on one NVIDIA DGX Spark. The first adapter is trained by next-token prediction on a 61.6-million-token corpus covering ten engineering themes. The corpus was built from 13,879 source documents, of which 7,069 were retained after deduplication and a two-tier keyword filter that removes cross-domain lexical collisions. Its validation loss falls from 2.082 to 1.976 over 1,500 steps. Direct testing showed that this adapter could still drift off topic on a retrieval-grounded ballast-water prompt, so we trained a second adapter on 2,295 question-answer pairs (114 hand-written and 2,181 generated by the base model from corpus passages) with the loss restricted to answer tokens. On 20 held-out prompts scored by hand for accuracy, topicality and specificity (maximum 120), the plain base model, the continuation adapter, the instruction adapter and the instruction adapter with retrieval scored 42, 56, 84 and 88. Absolute accuracy stays low (14 of 40 without retrieval and 20 of 40 with it). We report the full pipeline, two negative results (a reverted keyword fix and an instruction run that overfit within 100 steps), and the limits of the evaluation, which uses one small prompt set, no inter-rater agreement measure and model-generated reference answers.

title: Geometric Stability and Sample Complexity for Compositional Function Priors
summary: We study when compositional structure yields dimension reduction in supervised learning. We frame learning as empirical risk minimization with a function-space prior: a regularization functional selects a subset of functions with favorable approximation and metric entropy. The models are compositions $f(x)=g(Ax+Δh(x))$, where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$ is a linear base map, $Δh$ is a nonlinear correction, and $g$ is an outer function; that is, $f$ is an arbitrary smooth function of a $k$-dimensional representation of the input that is linear up to a correction. We prove covering-number bounds showing that the statistical complexity of this class interpolates between an intrinsic regime, parametric in the $kd$ entries of the linear map and nonparametric only in the representation dimension $k$, and an ambient $d$-dimensional nonparametric rate; the interpolation is controlled by the correction size $\varepsilon=\|Δh\|$. We then connect $\varepsilon$ to data geometry. If the data lie in a small tube around a $k$-dimensional manifold and the regression target depends on the input only through its nearest point on that manifold, then locally the target factorizes exactly as $g(Ax+Δh(x))$ with $A$ a tangent chart and a correction whose Sobolev norm scales linearly with curvature at the localization scale. Patching such local models over an atlas gives a finite-sample excess-risk bound for a least-squares estimator over a finite net of local models, whose ambient term vanishes with curvature. For a one-dimensional model problem we also prove a converse: on curved data, every affine compositional predictor faces an error floor unless its correction budget scales with curvature, while the matching curved model class attains the intrinsic rate. The correction size $\varepsilon$ is thus the effective-dimension parameter linking curvature to statistical complexity.
comment: 25 pages. An extended abstract was accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations (NeurReps), non-archival. Ancillary file: companion document with extended proofs and examples

title: Self-Calibrating Vision-Agent-Action: Deploying Pick-and-Place to New Robot Cells without Demonstrations or Fine-Tuning
summary: In simulation, Vision-Agent-Action (VAA) performs pick-and-place in robot cells with gripper or base-frame changes without robot demonstrations or fine-tuning. It uses pre-trained vision-language and language models for interpretation, measures the command map and camera geometry from its own motion and fingertips, estimates lens distortion, and plans grasps from measured object depth. A controlled study of eight public LIBERO-fine-tuned vision-language-action models (VLAs) varies robot hardware, camera geometry, appearance, and base frame. Gripper and frame changes dominate their losses in the tested fractional design. Across 18 cells with these changes, frozen VAA achieves 230/360 successes (64%), the refined VAA 268/360 (74%), and the strongest released VLA on this subset 76/360 (21%). Paired ablations support the self-calibration bundle, lens estimation under compounded changes, and the measured-depth pipeline. On a two-step LIBERO-Goal chain with object state carried between instructions, VAA completes 54/60 chains in changed cells, while four evaluated VLAs complete none.

title: From zero-target transfer to target-site personalization: multi-source training across fall-detection models
summary: Video-based fall detection could support timely assistance when a person cannot call for help. Unfamiliar cameras and scarce local labels challenge deployment. We examine whether joint training improves cross-dataset detection and subsequent local training. We analyze 2,697 clips from eight OmniFall datasets and one AI-Hub dataset. Positive clips contain a fall or collapse transition, while negative clips do not. We hold out each dataset in turn, training on the other eight. We evaluate three vision-language models (VLMs), Qwen, LLaVA, and InternVL, and three visual baselines, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN. We evaluate the stored source model without target data for training or selection. For each label budget, we update a separate copy using labeled clips from the held-out target dataset. We call this target-site personalization. We compare the Source-initialized model with Target-only, which skips source training but uses identical target clips and updates. Across nine targets, source training raises mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) from frozen-model values of 0.821 to 0.912 for Qwen, 0.883 to 0.947 for LLaVA, and 0.939 to 0.962 for InternVL. With five target examples per class and 26 updates per run, 95% confidence intervals for the AUROC benefit over Target-only lie above zero for Qwen, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN. With full-target training, they lie above zero only for Qwen and LLaVA. Separate VLM analyses reveal threshold sensitivity and post-fall false detections. The benefit varies by model and label budget.

title: Gradient-Based Co-Design of Systems and Reinforcement Learning Policies with Differentiable Simulators
summary: Co-design is the problem of jointly optimizing the design of a system and the policy that operates it. Neither can be chosen independently: a system design is only as good as the policy trained for it, and the optimal policy changes with the design. When that policy is learned by reinforcement learning (RL), evaluating a candidate design requires a full policy training run, and the design is usually optimized by black-box search such as Bayesian optimization (BO) or evolution strategies (ES). These methods scale poorly with the design dimension and ignore the differentiable structure of modern simulators and, in particular, the sensitivity of the optimal policy with respect to the design. We instead derive a gradient-based co-design method, where the design gradient decomposes into a direct effect of changing the design at a fixed policy and an indirect effect through the design-dependent optimal policy. The indirect effect requires the sensitivity of the converged policy to the design, which we obtain by applying the implicit function theorem to the stationarity condition of the policy gradient. Based on this sensitivity, we develop a proof-of-concept co-design algorithm with stochastic value gradient (SVG)-style policy optimization, prove that it converges to an approximately stationary design, and demonstrate on a differentiable networked-system benchmark with high-dimensional design spaces that it consistently outperforms BO and ES.

title: Grokking Can Be Steered: Selecting Desirable Solutions By Choice Of Learning Rule
summary: During grokking, a network transitions from memorization to generalization, yet what shapes the neural implementation (circuit) of the generalizing solution and specifically the number of participating neurons (its size) remains unclear. We find that the learning rule, the combination of credit assignment algorithm and optimizer, controls this: On modular addition, every learning rule we study that groks recovers the same Fourier-based algorithm, yet implemented by circuits that differ in size. Why? A neuron stays in use when its credit is large relative to the non-gradient term of its own update, and this single condition unifies three routes to unused neurons: the coupled weight decay, Adam's $ε$ and the decay of a trainable per-neuron gain. Equalizing the magnitude of credit assigned to each neuron, or scaling each neuron's weight decay by its credit, expands the effective circuit size, measured from the outgoing weights, from 60% to 99% of the layer's neurons at similar training and test accuracy. We vary which neurons share one equalization factor, from the whole layer to individual neurons, and find that the circuit stays concentrated for groups of eight or more and fully distributes only when every neuron has its own factor. Credit magnitudes are usually set by the normalization of standard optimizers: Nero, which normalizes per neuron, distributes the computation, whereas Adam and seven others, including RMSProp, Muon, and Shampoo, use other normalization schemes and retain small, concentrated circuits. Distributed circuits tolerate neuron deletion better, while concentrated circuits can be pruned further and transfer about twice as fast to a task that recombines the same features, largely by recruiting their unused neurons. Learning rule choice thus steers circuit size, trading robustness against compressibility and transfer speed without changing the learned algorithm.

title: Assume/Guarantee Contracts for the Compositional Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning of Heterogeneous Teams
summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems for heterogeneous teams require agents to collaborate to complete team tasks while making the best use of diverse agent capabilities. We introduce assume/guarantee contracts for heterogeneous multi-agent systems (AGC-MAS) and Iterative Heterogeneous Assignment for MARL (IHA-MARL). AGC-MAS contracts are compositional objects that encode the assumptions provided to, and the guarantees required of, each subtask contributing to the overall team task. We formulate contracts as tuples that specify a subtask, an automaton, timeout and success-probability requirements, and dispatch behavior. The automaton tracks an agent's high-level progress through the subtask associated with its contract and provides a natural mechanism for synchronization across contracts. Our abstraction enables robust interaction across heterogeneous low-level subtask implementations, allows heterogeneous agents to substitute for one another in satisfying contracts, and supports reuse of previously satisfied contracts in new team contexts. Having defined our theoretical framework, we develop a decomposition algorithm that breaks down a team task into a set of contracts. We then propose an iterative algorithm for task assignment and MARL that alternates between assigning contracts representing subtasks to individual agents, training the assigned agents to satisfy their contracts, and assessing their resulting capabilities to inform the next round of task assignments until the team's success probability meets the desired threshold. Our experimental results demonstrate the versatility of contracts in enabling agent substitution and contract reuse. Across three benchmarks with five seeds each, IHA-MARL achieves observed $100\%$ final evaluation success. In CPU timing pilots, comparable baselines required approximately $7$--$11\times$ more training-loop time.

title: ImpedanceMimic: Learned Impedance as Action Space for Force-Accurate Motion Imitation
summary: Recovering the forces behind a motion is ill-posed: different controllers can reproduce the same movement while generating different contact forces. Physics-based motion imitation resolves this ambiguity through simulation, but relies on fixed-gain proportional-derivative (PD) control. We show that fixed gains impose a trade-off between motion and force tracking, as contact and swing place conflicting demands on joint stiffness and damping. We introduce ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning policy that modulates per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements, but requires only motion at inference. Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms matched fixed-gain PD under every integration scheme, direct-torque, muscle-actuated and existing imitation controllers in kinematic and force fidelity, approaching a dedicated motion-to-force regressor. By expressing gains as multiples of inertia-scaled priors, a single policy controls subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric input and transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot. The learned impedance forms a low-dimensional representation of motor state, shared across bodies, that generalizes to withheld activities: stiffness scales with load, and damping anticipates unloading.

title: Beyond Alignment: Supervising the Generator for EEG-to-Image Reconstruction
summary: Visual brain decoding translates neural activity into human-interpretable images. While recent EEG-to-image reconstruction methods rely on aligning EEG signals with pretrained visual embeddings to condition an image generator, we empirically demonstrate that stronger cross-modal alignment do not translate into comparable gains in reconstruction quality. This indicates that improving the input condition alone is insufficient; the generative process itself requires explicit supervision. Although Representation Alignment (REPA) offers a solution by guiding diffusion transformers with pretrained vision encoder features, we find that EEG-conditioned generators struggle to follow these fixed targets. To address this mismatch, we introduce generation-derived supervision (GDS): an image-conditioned teacher that translates static image-encoder features into the internal representation space of a diffusion transformer. Our EEG-conditioned student generator closely tracks these dynamic targets during denoising, discarding the teacher at inference. Evaluated on THINGS-EEG and THINGS-MEG, our approach consistently outperforms conditioning-centric baselines, achieving state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity.

title: ReCALM: A Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism for Distributed Continual Service Construction
summary: Crowdsourcing has emerged as a promising paradigm for constructing AI services by harnessing the collective capabilities of distributed workers. As consumers' demands continually evolve, service models must acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned information. However, due to the inherited reliance on gradients for backpropagation, existing approaches typically suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual model updates on heterogeneous data. Recent studies have introduced analytic learning, a gradient-free paradigm that achieves invariance through recursive closed-form solutions. Nevertheless, existing analytic methods are typically constrained by single-layer linear networks, which tend to suffer from underfitting due to their inability to perform deep representation learning. To address this issue, we propose ReCALM, a Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism that achieves deep nonlinear invariance for distributed continual service construction. Inspired by the success of ResNet, we develop gradient-free residual blocks for ReCALM with closed-form solutions. To implement distributed continual training for ReCALM, we further devise a cross-recursive strategy via least squares. Both theoretical and experimental analyses verify ReCALM's dual superiority in heterogeneity invariance and deep representation. With 20 residual layers, ReCALM improves accuracy by 8.85%-9.83% over the single-layer analytic baseline, while reducing computational costs by over 94% compared with gradient-based baselines.

title: Hardware-Friendly Plug-and-Play MVDR Beamforming for Microphone Arrays: Algorithm, Prototype, and System-Level Feasibility
summary: Beamforming has been widely recognized for its spatial filtering capability in speech signal processing, enabling effective interference rejection and signal enhancement. The performance of adaptive beamforming methods, e.g., the conventional minimum variance distortionless response (MVDR) beamforming, often deteriorate significantly in complex and dynamic acoustic environments. Part of the reason is that such conventional beamforming ignores the intrinsic characteristics of speech. To address this issue, this paper proposes Plug-and-Play Minimum Variance Distortionless Response (PnP-MVDR) algorithm, which integrates data-driven speech prior information into the MVDR framework to enhance robustness against non-stationary noise while maintaining its interpretability. The PnP-MVDR framework supports joint interaction of signal processing and deep learning methods and is designed to be compatible with modern DSP-NPU architectures, making it hardware-friendly for potential edge deployment. Beyond the algorithmic innovation, we have developed a complete microphone beamforming system to validate practical feasibility. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms traditional and deep learning-based baselines, establishing PnP-MVDR as an effective and deployable solution for edge audio scenarios.

title: AcousticBEV: Acoustic BEV Object Localization for Intelligent Vehicles
summary: Modern autonomous driving and driver assistance systems rely predominantly on cameras, radars and LiDARs for environmental perception. However, these modalities face different environmental limitations, including poor illumination for cameras and adverse weather for LiDAR. Acoustic sensing, particularly using microphone arrays, could provide complementary perception capabilities for autonomous driving, but has remained largely underexplored. In this work, we design a horizontally arranged microphone array that functions as the "ears" of a vehicle, enabling localization of nearby moving vehicles in a bird's-eye view (BEV) representation that captures both their relative direction and distance. Using this array, we collect a real-world driving dataset, AcousticScenes, which contains 2,117 static and 2,863 dynamic samples with synchronized spatial acoustic signals, LiDAR point clouds and 3D bounding box annotations. Building on this dataset, we propose AcousticBEV, a learning-based method for acoustic BEV object localization, which estimates the center locations of moving traffic participants in BEV from the microphone-array signals, conditioned on the ego vehicle's own speed. Experimental results demonstrate that AcousticBEV outperforms both classical signal-processing baselines and other learning-based methods, achieving F1 scores of $47.7 \pm 1.2$% on "Easy" scenarios and $45.1 \pm 1.4$% on "Difficult" cases. Our findings demonstrate that acoustic signals from a low-cost, vehicle-mounted microphone array can localize nearby moving vehicles in both azimuth and distance.

title: With the Right Representation, Classical Machine Learning Rivals Deep Models for Olfactory Mixture Similarity
summary: Modeling olfactory mixtures remains a critical challenge in machine olfaction because the task requires reasoning over relationships between sets of odorants rather than over individual molecules in isolation. However, prior comparisons between deep and classical approaches also varied how the relationship between the two mixtures was represented, since the classical baselines primarily relied on weak representations that described each mixture independently and provided little direct signal about how the mixtures differed. In this work, we revisit classical learning using explicit symmetric comparison features on unordered pairs of mixtures, evaluating these representations with XGBoost and kernel ridge regression (KRR). We find that XGBoost with explicit comparison features achieves performance competitive with specialized deep mixture models on the main benchmark. Ablation studies show that coordinate-wise absolute differences alone provide strong predictive performance, while combining them with sums and products yields further improvements. KRR also benefits substantially from explicit comparison features, with further gains from appropriate kernel choice and preprocessing. Overall, these results suggest that explicitly encoding how two mixtures differ is an important ingredient for classical machine learning in low-data olfactory mixture prediction.

title: SuperGlance: Driving at a Glance with a Vision-Language Model
summary: Autonomous driving is turning to vision-language-action models (VLAs). They answer and plan by decoding, one step at a time. Each step is another forward pass, so a plan can take over a second of GPU time. Embodied AI often pairs such a slow, reasoning System 2 with a fast System 1 that acts. Human drivers plan at a glance, with System 1. Faster designs usually put System 1 outside the vision-language model (VLM), in a planner without its abilities. Yet before a VLM writes its first token, it has already read the scene into one hidden state. We show that, once trained, this hidden state is enough to drive and to answer questions about what the model sees. SuperGlance reads it to turn a decoder-only VLM into an encoder-style driving policy. Its linear head scores a fixed set of 5,273 candidate trajectories. With the set fixed, rewards are computed offline, so supervised targets can be reward-weighted and reinforcement learning maximizes the exact expected reward. Before and during policy training, multiple-choice training keeps the VLM's visual abilities in one pass, so the policy still answers questions about driving scenes. Training questions are built against shortcuts. Each must be answered right in two option orders. Against drift, a KL term keeps each stage near its starting model. One pass offers VLAs a more plausible path to System 1. SuperGlance answers visual multiple-choice questions as well as its base VLM does by decoding. It plans in 84 ms of GPU time, six times faster than Qwen-Drive-1.0, and at least as well on NAVSIM, PAI-AV and WOD-E2E. In AlpaSim closed loop, km per at-fault incident holds for both planners up to a 300-ms delay and drops beyond. With GPU time charged as delay, SuperGlance's lead over Qwen-Drive-1.0 grows from 2.8 to 3.9 times. Delayed by 1.2 s, our model falls below Qwen-Drive-1.0 at its own 518 ms.

title: GameWM: Toward Next-Generation Video Games with Interaction-Centric World Models
summary: For more than half a century, video games have pursued better graphics, more natural interaction, and more engaging gameplay. Generative video models (VMs) now bear on all three. Neural networks already draw most of the pixels in shipped games, and recent world models let a lightweight game engine keep the world state while a VM turns the engine's coarse proxy video into final frames. These systems, however, treat the VM as a renderer that only restyles motion the engine has already authored, which leaves most of its generative capacity unused and limits the diversity a game can offer. We present GameWM, a design for next-generation games built on a clear division of labor. The GameWM-engine keeps what must be exact: rules, state, camera, and the layout of the world, which also spares the video model from having to remember it. The GameWM-VM generates what is expensive to author by hand: the look of the world and the detail of the player's interactions. One game mechanic can then be realized in many visually and physically distinct ways, while its outcome stays exactly as the engine computed it. To realize this division of labor, we build GameWM as a complete system: a data engine centered on interactions rather than exploration, an interface through which authored character sheets, scene art, and skill descriptions enter the model, and a model family from 5B to 33B parameters with a real-time causal variant for play. Together they give every player a fresh version of the same game: each player's own character, world, and skills turn the same engine mechanics into a new experience, while every event keeps the timing and outcome the GameWM-engine computed.

title: Hardening Agentic Web Populations Through Multi-Criterion Competitive Co-Evolution: Lessons from Wargame Strategy Optimization
summary: Agents on the open web will face adversaries that keep adapting, so a defense that is only tested once will eventually be found and broken. We propose treating jailbreak attacks and safety guardrails as two populations that evolve against each other, rather than as a fixed attacker probing a fixed defense. This idea comes directly from wargame strategy optimization, where two-population competitive co-evolution with alternating evolution cycles and cross-play evaluation has already been shown to produce strategies that are robust to a moving opponent, and where a companion line of work has shown that the same machinery can measure how much competitive pressure a population must absorb. However, real-world applications can never rely on a single criterion as a key performance indicator, rather must use multiple conflicting criteria, such as, cost and efficiency. We describe how this mechanism transfers to language model safety, argue why the resulting multi-criteria, competitive and coevolutionary arms race is a genuinely networked, population-level problem rather than a two-agent toy setting, and lay out the open problems that stand between the wargame version of this idea and an agentic web version of it.
comment: Accepted at the 1st NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agentic Web: Decentralized, Continually-Adapting Agent Ecosystems (https://neurips.cc/virtual/2026/loc/atlanta/174837)

title: Learning Graph-Conditioned Predictors in Weight Space
summary: The same node attributes can imply different labels in different structural contexts. Yet fast graphless models typically treat topology as additional evidence supplied to a globally shared predictor. This assumes that structure augments the available information, rather than determining how node attributes should be interpreted. We introduce SCOPE (Structure-COnditioned PrEdictor), in which a small generator maps each node's cached structural fingerprint to coefficients over a shared low-rank basis, producing a context-specific update to a global weight matrix. The base predictor, basis, and generator remain shared across all nodes, while the resulting transformation adapts how attributes are processed in each relational environment. Once fingerprints are cached, inference requires only a forward pass and no online message passing. This design combines context-specific specialization with global parameter sharing, compact low-rank adaptation, and message-passing-free inference. On two large OGB node-classification graphs, conditioning the weights with raw positional signals yields clear gains over supplying the same signals through input concatenation. Further results under a structure-transductive held-out-node protocol and in teacher-free graph classification show that the mechanism extends beyond a particular distillation setting. These findings establish graph structure not only as predictive evidence, but as context that determines the predictor used to interpret that evidence.

title: WA-JEPA: Goal-Aware Predictive Feedback Action Refinement for a World-Action Model
summary: JEPA-based world models predict action consequences in latent space, but representative planning approaches rely on candidate-action search, requiring repeated evaluation of action sequences and incurring substantial online computational cost. Direct action generation avoids this search, yet how to leverage latent predictions to guide action generation given task goals remains a key challenge in translating learned physical dynamics into effective decisions. We introduce WA-JEPA, a world-action model that couples action generation, action-conditioned latent prediction, and goal-aware feedback. The model first generates an action proposal and predicts the resulting future scenes and proprioceptive states, then refines the proposal through two complementary feedback paths, using the task goal as a reference. Goal-discrepancy residual feedback (GDRF) uses differences between the latent representations of predicted scenes and the task goal to guide chunk-wise action refinement. Future-scene context feedback (FSCF) preserves fine-grained predicted scene representations to guide subsequent action refinement. Jointly learned from offline demonstrations, this process iteratively updates the same plan before execution, making future predictions directly participate in action generation without candidate-action search. We evaluate short-horizon goal reaching, long-horizon tasks, and full-task execution. The results show that goal-aware predictive feedback supports competitive task performance while maintaining a compact model and low online computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/Dovisya/WA-JEPA.

title: MARS: Dynamic Routing of Reinforcement-Learned Atomic Skills for Multi-Stage Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in multi-task robotic manipulation. However, they still face limitations in control precision and execution stability during critical manipulation stages, such as object grasping, alignment and insertion. To combine general-purpose manipulation capabilities with task-specific fine-grained control, while enabling effective coordination between generalist and specialized policies throughout multi-stage manipulation tasks, this paper proposes MARS (Modular Atomic-skill Routing System), a dynamic routing framework for reinforcement learning-based atomic skills. MARS integrates a frozen generalist VLA policy with multiple independently trained atomic skill policies. Using a shared RL Token state representation and the reference action of VLA, specialized control policies are optimized through reinforcement learning for different cr`itical manipulation stages. For high-level policy selection, we develop a dynamic router that integrates temporal context and skill semantics. The router employs Mamba-based recurrent encoding and a historical feature window to capture state evolution during manipulation. Skill descriptions of candidate policies are encoded into semantic queries, and attention mechanisms are used to establish correspondences between skill semantics and temporal state features. Experimental results show that MARS achieves an average Macro-F1 score of 90.47% across four LIBERO task suites under fixed-trajectory evaluation, outperforming an MLP-based router by 7.08 percentage points. In the simulated Tube Transport task, the full-task success rate increases from 20.04% to 85.67%. These results demonstrate that stage-specific reinforcement learning and temporal state-aware dynamic policy routing can improve multi-policy coordination and overall task execution performance in multi-stage robotic manipulation.

title: Distilling Safety Filters for Filter-free Multi-agent RL
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can teach robot teams to navigate shared spaces, but trial and error causes collisions that real robots cannot afford. Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters prevent these collisions by correcting unsafe actions, yet in a team the filter becomes a centralized optimization whose number of constraints grows quadratically with the team size. We propose an approach that builds the filter's safety into the RL policy and examine how such a system behaves during filter-free deployment. However, the filter that keeps training safe also hides what the policy must learn: it masks the cost of unsafe actions, which actor-critic methods then overvalue, and it keeps near-collision states out of the training data. Our approach therefore learns only from executed safe actions with implicit Q-learning and distills the filter into the policy at synthetic near-collision states. We prove that filter distillation loss bounds the policy's constraint violation and hence how far agents can cross their safety margin, so errors never accumulate. When distillation states cover deployed states, the loss also bounds the collision probability at every step. Without a filter and acting only on local observations, our policies have no collisions in 1,800 test episodes with multiple agents. A policy trained with three agents transfers zero-shot to teams of twenty at constant per-agent computation and stays collision-free with up to eight agents. We test our policies on Crazyflie quadrotors with up to five flying at the same time.

title: CausalGloss: Multi-Evidence Action Control for a Simultaneous Mandarin Speech-to-ASL Gloss Cascade
summary: Simultaneous Mandarin speech-to-American Sign Language (ASL) gloss translation requires deciding when an evolving utterance supports committing each gloss. Fixed Wait-k cannot adapt to source-gloss reordering, while training only on reference histories causes exposure bias. We present CausalGloss, an English-prefix-to-ASL-gloss action policy for a Mandarin-speech cascade. It combines lexical and semantic evidence, bounded delay, negation constraints, burst WRITE actions, and incomplete-history recovery. On a frozen 500-example How2Sign-derived benchmark with weak LLM-generated references, CausalGloss improves the fixed Wait-k frontier and nearly matches a three-seed TransLLaMA-style learned adaptive baseline at k = 5 in Token F1 (0.7047 versus 0.7067), with 54.4% lower LAAL. Against CLERC Epee human-gloss references, it achieves 0.649 Token F1 and Pareto-dominates three-seed TransLLaMA-style k = 5 and fixed k = 5, 7, reducing LAAL by 58.2-69.9%. Ablations separate timing from retention. A synthetic Mandarin-speech cascade preserves a smaller computation-aware latency gain, although outputs remain over-long. We also construct ChineseSpeech-ASLGloss-v1, a 19,924-utterance, 36.54-h controlled evaluation corpus.
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE ICASSP 2027

title: Before the Word: Name Information in Description-Derived States of Small Language Models, With and Without Naming Failure
summary: The tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state, knowing an object but not its name, motivates this study as an analogy only. We ask whether small language models form a name-predictive state from a name-free description, and whether it differs when naming fails but description selection succeeds. In an internally pre-registered study (a frozen document, no external registry) of Qwen2-0.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B and Phi-3-mini with 200 items, we combine a similarity read-out, a Patchscopes-style read-out and activation patching with matched controls. H1 (name information in the state) was supported in all nine model-by-description-type combinations; the agreement rule was met by the similarity measure together with patching, while Patchscopes stayed near chance. Post-hoc robustness checks after internal review (logit lens, single-position patch, manipulation check) temper this reading: name information in middle layers is clearest under the multi-position patch and the similarity measure, and weak under single-position patching at 50% depth. H2' (description-paraphrase consistency of name-free states not lower in failure items) is mixed: the SmolLM2 deficit test is significant under the pre-registered specification but not robust; Phi-3 non-inferiority holds across margins and a word-overlap covariate, although its bootstrap interval includes zero; Qwen2-0.5B is inconclusive. A capacity explanation remains untested. We report vehicle-level signals only, not meaning.
